title: Rajesh Kumar vs . State Of Gujarat, 1(2012) Crimes 500; ... on 7 December, 2021
full_text: Rajesh Kumar vs . State Of Gujarat, 1(2012) Crimes 500; ... on 7 December, 2021 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 IN THE COURT OF MS. TWINKLE CHAWLA: MM, NI ACT-02, SOUTH- EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURTS COMPLEX: NEW DELHI Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder CC No.7310/2017 U/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 1. CIS number : DLSE020165392017 2. Name of the Complainant : Banarsi Dass Saini 3. Name of the Accused, : Inder S/o. Sh. Ganga Dass, R/o. Village parentage & residential Manoli, District Ghaziabad, U.P. address 4. Offence complained of or : U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act , proved 1881 5. Plea of the Accused : Pleaded not guilty and claimed trial 6. Final Judgment/order : CONVICTED 7. Date of judgment/order : 07.12.2021 JUDGMENT 1. Complainant has filed the present complaint under Section 138 / 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (" NI Act ") on the averments that, the Accused and Complainant are brothers and the Complainant advanced a loan of Rs. 12,50,000/- to the Accused for the purposes of purchasing property, which was to be returned Page 1 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 within six months. 2. As per the Complainant, the Accused in repayment of the said loan issued a post- dated cheque bearing No. 254761 dt. 25.05.2013 drawn on Oriental Bank of Commerce, Sultanpur Branch, Ghaziabad, for an amount of Rs. 12,50,000/- in favour of the Complainant (hereinafter referred as "cheque in question"). As per the Complainant, the cheque in question was given to the Complainant on 13.01.2013. However, when the Complainant presented the cheque in question; the same was returned unpaid vide return memo dated 06.08.2013, for the reason "insufficient funds". The Complainant sent the legal demand notice dated 13.08.2013 through his counsel by speed post at the registered address of the Accused. Hence, despite the service of the legal demand notice Accused failed to make the payment and the Complainant filed the present complaint. 3. After taking pre-summoning evidence, Accused was ordered to be summoned in this case for commission of offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (" NI Act "), vide order dated 17.09.2013. 4. Accused appeared and was released on bail on 02.07.2018. On finding a prima facie case, notice U/s 251 of the Criminal Procedure Code , 1973 (" CrPC ") was served upon the Accused on 02.07.2018 to which he pleaded not guilty and opted to contest after disclosing the following defence: "I am the signatory of the impugned cheque. Me and the Complainant are real brothers. My father, Late. Sh. Ganga Dass executed a will whereby I was given a property. Thus, the Complainant bore a grudge against me. The Complainant visited my house where I had kept my cheque book containing blank signed cheques. The impugned cheque was stolen by Complainant and thereafter misused. I did not receive legal notice." 5. Vide order dated 25.09.2018, opportunity was granted to the Accused to cross Page 2 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 examine the Complainant. The Complainant/CW1 adopted his pre summoning evidence affidavit Ex. CW1/H and also proved following documents: Ex. Cheque bearing no. 254671 dated CW1/B: 25.05.2013 of Rs.12,50,000/-. Ex. Return memo issued by bank dt. 06.08.2013. CW1/C: Ex. Legal Demand notice dt. 13.08.2013. CW1/D: Ex. Postal receipt dt. 13.08.2013 in respect of CW1/E: legal demand notice. Ex. Return envelope of legal demand notice CW1/F: indicating refusal of receipt of demand notice. Ex. Complaint U/s. 138 R/w. 142 NI Act . CW1/G: During cross-examination of the Complainant, the Complainant also produced and proved Ex.CW1/X, i.e., a receipt dt. 16.01.2013 executed by the Accused and Ex.CW1/Y, i.e., the statement of account of the Complainant and Ex.CW1/D1, which is a will executed by Sh. Ganga Das. Complainant Evidence was closed vide separate statement on 31.07.2019. 6. Thereafter, Accused was examined under Section 313 of CrPC for explaining the circumstances appearing against him in the Complainant's evidence. He denied the Complainant's case and pleaded false implication in the present case and opted to lead evidence in his defence. 7. However, the Accused despite opportunity did not lead any DE; and defence evidence was closed by way of court order on 21.01.2020. Thereafter, application of the Accused to lead DE was dismissed by way of order dt. 13.02.2020. Applications filed by Accused U/s. 311 CrPC and Section 73 Indian Evidence Act were also disposed of and dismissed vide order dt. 10.09.2020. 8. I have heard Ld. Counsel for the parties and have perused the case file along with Page 3 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 the written submissions filed by the parties carefully and meticulously. Submissions of the Complainant and Accused 9. The Ld. Counsel for the Complainant has submitted that all ingredients of Section 138 NI Act are fulfilled in the present case and hence, the presumption under Section 139 NI Act arises in the favour of the Complainant, which has not been successfully rebutted by the Accused. 10.Per contra, Ld. Counsel for the Accused has submitted that the Accused deserves to be acquitted as the Complainant has failed to prove the return memo, given that the same does not bear the stamp/seal of the bank and the bank witness has not been examined to prove the same. Reliance has been placed on the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Bombay in Smt. Vandana v. Smt. Abhilasha, CRL . Appeal No. 360/2017 and judgment of Hon'ble Gujarat High Court in Rajendra Kumar @ Rajesh Kumar Vs. State of Gujarat, 1(2012) crimes 500; in favour of this contention. Ld. Counsel for the Accused during course of arguments has further submitted that the Complainant has misused the cheques stolen from the Accused due to spite towards the Accused as the Complainant was left out from the will of their father. Hence, as per the Ld. Counsel for the Accused, the Accused has rebutted the presumption by way of preponderance of probabilities. Legal Framework Ingredients of Section 138 NI Act: 11.The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Kusum Ingots & Alloys Ltd and Ors v. K Pennar Peterson Securities Ltd and Ors. , (2000) 2 SCC 745 ("Kusum Ingots Case"), has clearly stipulated that "the ingredients which are to be satisfied for making out a case under the provision are: (i) a person must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him in a bank for payment of a certain amount of money to another person from out Page 4 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 of that account for the discharge of any debt or other liability; (ii) that cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months1 from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier; (iii) that cheque is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of the account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with the bank; (iv) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within 152 days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (v) the drawer of such cheque fails to make payment of the said amount of money to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice; If the aforementioned ingredients are satisfied then the person who has drawn the cheque shall be deemed to have committed an offence." 12.Therefore, if the aforesaid ingredients are made out, the Accused is deemed to have committed an offence under Section 138 NI Act. Presumption under Section 139 NI Act/ Section 118 NI Act: 13. Section 139 NI Act states that: "Presumption in favour of holder: It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to 1 Reduced to three months vide RBI circular dated 4.11.2011. 2 The same is now enhanced to 30 days. Page 5 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability" 14. Section 139 NI Act is a type of reverse onus clause, which stipulates a presumption in the favour of the Complainant as to fact of a cheque being received in discharge of a legal debt or liability. 15.Further, Section 118(a) of the NI Act, states as follows: "Presumptions as to negotiable instruments. -- Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: (a) of consideration --that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;" 16.The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has in a number of judgments dealt with the combined effect of the presumptions raised under Section 139 and Section 118(a) NI Act. 17.The following proposition can be summarized on a perusal of the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Sunil Todi & Ors v. State of Gujarat , LL 2021 SC 706, Kalamani Tex v. P. Balasubramanian , 2021 SCC OnLine SC 75; APS Forex Services Pvt. Ltd. v. Shakti International Fashion Linkers and Ors. , AIR 2020 SC 945; Rohitbhai Jivanlal Patel v. State of Gujarat and Ors., AIR 2019 SC 1876 ("Rohitbhai Case"); Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets , (2009) 2 SCC 513 ("Kumar Exports Case"); K.N. Beena v. Muniyappan and Anr. , (2001) 8 SCC 458; and Dhanvantrai Balwantrai Desai v. State of Maharashtra , 1964 Cri. LJ 437: (i) Once the execution of cheque is admitted; Section 139 of the NI Act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of legally Page 6 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 enforceable debt or liability; (ii) The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the Accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities; (iii) Something which is probable has to be brought on record by the Accused for getting the burden of proof shifted to the Complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the Accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their non-existence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist; (iv) The words "unless the contrary is proved" which occur in Section 139 , make it clear that the presumption has to be rebutted by 'proof' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, therefore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by Section 139 NI Act cannot be said to be rebutted; (v) To rebut the presumption, it is open for the Accused to rely on evidence led by him or Accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the Complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely; (vi) That it is not necessary for the Accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence, Section 139 imposed an evidentiary burden and not a Page 7 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 persuasive burden. Analysis 18.In the case at hand, it is not in dispute that the cheque in question was drawn by the Accused from his bank account. Further, it is also not in dispute that the Accused is the signatory of the cheque in question as in the defence disclosed by the Accused U/s 251 CrPC and Section 313 CrPC statement; he has duly admitted the same. Presentation of the cheque in question by the Complainant is also not in dispute. 19.The dishonour of the cheque in question by way of the return memo, Ex. CW1/C, has been disputed by the Ld. Counsel for the Accused in the course of arguments. It has been stated that presumption U/s. 146 NI Act cannot be drawn as the return memo does not bear the stamp and seal of the bank. It has further been argued that while the Complainant has in his evidence affidavit as well as the complaint, stated that the returning memo is dated as of 05.08.2013; and that the cheque was deposited through his bank, namely, Canara Bank; the return memo attached to the complaint, i.e., Ex. CW1/C is dated 06.08.2013 and has been issued by the Accused Bank. Hence, it is the submission of the Ld. Counsel for the Accused that the said return memo is a manufactured one, since it is not possible for the Accused bank to issue a return memo later than the memo furnished by Complainant bank. It is firstly noted that the Ex. CW1/C bears the signature of the bank official, though the same is not stamped. Further, the perusal of the complaint and evidence affidavit shows that the Complainant has not specified the bank from which the return memo was issued on 05.08.2013, i.e., the bank of the Complainant or the Accused. Upon inquiry, Ld. Counsel for the Complainant has submitted that Ex. CW1/C is the only return memo received by the Complainant and the mention of 05.08.2013 instead of 06.08.2013 is a typographical error. It is further noted that throughout the trial, it has never been the case of the Accused that the cheque in question was never dishonoured, or that he had sufficient funds in his account on the said of dishonour and hence, the cheque in question would have been cleared. Hence, in view of the Page 8 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 fact that Ex. CW1/C has been signed by the bank official; and that the Ex. CW1/C along with the fact of dishonour has been duly sworn by the Complainant in his affidavit Ex.CW1/H and that no evidence to the contrary has been brough by the Accused; it is noted that the cheque in question was returned unpaid for the reason "Insufficient Funds". 20.The Complainant sent the legal demand notice, dated 13.08.2013 (Ex. CW1/D) by way of speed post (Ex. CW1/E (Colly)). The service of the same was refused by the Accused, which is evinced by the endorsement on the return envelope, i.e., Ex.CW1/F. It is trite law that refusal is deemed service. Though, it is the stand of the Accused that he has not received the legal demand notice; but it is noted that in response to question in statement U/s. 313 CrPC with respect to the legal demand notice, the Accused has, while denying the receipt of the same, stated that "the address mentioned in the legal demand notice is my correct address". Further the address mentioned in the legal demand notice has been mentioned by the Accused in his bail bond as well. Hence, the legal demand notice was sent on the correct address of the Accused. Therefore, a presumption of due service is drawn u/s 27 of General Clauses Act, 1897; which provides that where the notice is sent by registered post to the correct address, the same shall be presumed to have been duly served. In M/s Darbar Exports and other v. Bank of India, 2003 (2) SCC (NI) 132 (Delhi), the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi held that a presumption of service of notice is to be drawn where the notice is sent through registered post as well as UPC on correct address. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Hazi v. Palapetty Muhammad & Anr , (2007) 6SCC 555 has held that: "Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in respect of the complaint U/s 138 of the Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submit to the court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with summons) and, therefore, the complaint is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the court along with the copy of complaint U/s 138 of Page 9 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required U/s 138, by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary U/s 27 of the General Clauses Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act.". 21.Thus, the legal demand notice Ex. CW1/D is held to have been duly served upon the Accused. Finally, the complaint has been filed within the limitation period. Therefore, essential ingredients (i) to (v) as stipulated by the Hon'ble SC in Kusum Ingots Case (supra), have been duly satisfied. 22. Further, as noted above, once the execution of the cheque by the Accused is proved/admitted, the presumption of the same being drawn for consideration stands attracted in terms of Section 139 NI Act. Now, in the case at hand, so far as the question of existence of basic ingredients for drawing of presumption U/s 118 (a) and 139 of the NI Act is concerned, from the aforesaid discussion, it is apparent that the Accused has not denied his signatures on the cheque in question that has been drawn in favour of the Complainant on a bank account maintained by the Accused; and hence the said presumption can be drawn. The Ld. Counsel for the Accused has stated that such inference cannot be drawn as the Complainant has stolen the cheque in the form of blank signed cheque and the particulars on the same have been filled by or at the instance of the Complainant. At this stage, reliance can be laid on the observations of the Hon'ble SC in Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar , (2019) 4 SCC 197; wherein it has been held that: "It is immaterial that the cheque may have been filled in by any person other than the drawer, if the cheque is duly signed by the drawer. If the cheque is otherwise valid, the penal provisions of Section 138 would be attracted... 38. If a signed blank cheque is voluntarily presented to a payee, towards some payment, the payee may fill up the amount and other particulars. This in itself would not invalidate the cheque. The onus would still be on Page 10 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 the Accused to prove that the cheque was not in discharge of a debt or liability by adducing evidence... 40. Even a blank cheque leaf voluntarily signed and handed over by the Accused, which is towards some payment, would attract presumption Under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, in the absence of any cogent evidence to show that the cheque was not issued in discharge of a debt." (emphasis supplied) 23.The same view has been endorsed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Ravi Chopra v. State, CRL.M.C. 5211/2006; wherein it was observed that: "A collective reading of the above provisions shows that even under the scheme of the NI Act it is possible for the drawer of a cheque to give a blank cheque signed by him to the payee and consent either impliedly or expressly to the said cheque being filled up at a subsequent point in time and presented for payment by the drawee. There is no provision in the NI Act which either defines the difference in the handwriting or the ink pertaining to the material particulars filled up in comparison with the signature thereon as constituting a "material alteration" for the purposes of Section 87 NI Act. What however is essential is that the cheque must have been signed by the drawer." (emphasis supplied) 24.Hence, in view of such clear stipulation by the Hon'ble Supreme Court and Hon'ble Delhi High Court, it is immaterial whether or not the particulars on the cheque have been filled by the Accused or not, to the extent the Accused has admitted to have appended his signatures on the cheque in question. Accordingly, the applicability of the presumption under Section 139 NI Act is not dependent upon the Accused filling Page 11 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 the particulars on the cheque. Accordingly, it is required to be presumed that the cheque in question were drawn for consideration and the holder of the cheque i.e., the Complainant received the same in discharge of an existing debt. The onus, therefore, shifts on the Accused to establish a probable defence so as to rebut such a presumption. 25.In the segment on legal framework, set out above, the legal proposition with respect to the burden of proof upon the Accused has already been discussed. Hence, it is now to be examined as to whether the Accused brought any material on record or pointed out glaring discrepancies in the material produced by the Complainant for dislodging the presumption which meets the standard of preponderance of probabilities. 26.The Accused in the present case, has taken the following line of defence with a view to rebut the presumption: (a) Misuse of stolen cheque: The Accused in his defence at the time of notice U/s. 251 CrPC stated that the Complainant has stolen his blank signed cheque and has misused the same. A similar suggestion was also given to the Complainant during his cross examination of the Complainant. Hence, the Accused has stated that he had no loan transaction with the Complainant. It is seen that the Accused has not led any defence evidence in the present complaint, including on this aspect. Further, during the cross examination of the Complainant, apart from a single suggestion as to the cheque having been stolen; no FIR, missing report etc. has been put to the Complainant. Hence, it appears that the Accused has not taken any legal action against the Complainant or otherwise; or sent any notice, written or otherwise to the Complainant qua the theft of the cheque in question. It is also noted that the reason for dishonour of the cheque in question is funds insufficient and not Page 12 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 payment stopped by drawer; which means that no stop instructions were issued by the Accused after the loss/theft of his signed blank cheque, as well. In addition to the above, it is also observed that apart from one suggestion as to the cheque having been stolen, no questions/suggestions have been put to the Complainant on his mode of procurement of the allegedly stolen/lost cheque in question. In fact, the Complainant in his cross-examination had deposed that the cheque in question was handed over to the Complainant by the Accused in the presence of the children of the Accused. However, the said persons have also not been examined by the Accused to support his defence of the theft of the cheque in question. It has been noted by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the Kumar Exports Case (supra), that the circumstantial evidence has to be seen from the point of a reasonable/prudent man. Further, the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in VS. Yadav v. Reena, 172 (2010) DLT 561, observed that: "In order to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of N.I. Act, the Accused, by cogent evidence, has to prove the circumstance under which cheques were issued. It was for the Accused to prove if no loan was taken why he did not write a letter to the Complainant for return of the cheque. Unless the Accused had proved that he acted like a normal businessman/prudent person entering into a contract he could not have rebutted the presumption under section 139 N.I. Act. If no loan was given but cheques were retained, he immediately would have protested and asked the cheques to be returned and if still cheques were not returned, he would have served a notice as Complainant. Nothing was proved in this case." (emphasis supplied) Similarly, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shree Daneshwari Traders v. Sanjay Jain & Anr. , AIR 2019 SC 4003, observed that: "the defence of the Respondent Page 13 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 that though he made payment for the commodities/rice bags, the blank cheques were not returned by the Appellant-Complainant is quite unbelievable and unacceptable." Accordingly, where the cheque in question was allegedly stolen by the Complainant, it does not appear reasonable/probable for a prudent man to not take any legal action or step against the theft of the same. No FIR has been lodged. Even after the receipt of the legal demand notice from the Complainant/summons from the Court qua the cheque in question, no legal proceedings have been stated to have been initiated against the Complainant by the Accused. Accordingly, the defence of the Accused as to the cheque in question being stolen is by way of mere assertion and only raises a possibility and not a probability and does not inspire confidence from the stand point of a reasonable man. (b) Absence of transaction between the Complainant and Accused: The Accused in his defence under Section 251 CrPC as well statement under Section 313 CrPC has denied the existence of the loan transaction with the Complainant. In the cross examination of the Complainant, Ld. Counsel for the Accused had put questions to the Complainant as to his financial capacity for grant of the loan. In order to prove the same, the Complainant has brought on record Ex.CW1/Y, which shows that an amount of Rs. 11,10,000/- was withdrawn by the Complainant on 23.01.2012, which is around the same time as the date of advancement of loan by the Complainant to the Accused. Hence, in light of the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa , (2019) 5 SCC 418, the Complainant has explained the source of funds, as being his retiral benefits. Further, Ld. Counsel for the Accused has stated that the receipt Ex.CW1/X brought by the Complainant is forged and fabricated and the signature on the same is not of the Accused. It is seen that no defence evidence has been led on this aspect and in the cross examination of the Page 14 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 Complainant apart from a similar question on the receipt been forged, no further cross examination has been done on this aspect. In fact, the Complainant has in his cross examination stated that the receipt is prepared by some boy called by the Accused; and attempted to explain the circumstances surrounding the execution of the receipt. In order to show that Ex. CW1/X is forged, no steps have been taken by the Accused. It has been submitted by the Accused during the course of arguments that he always signs as "Inder" and not "Inder Singh"; the latter being the signature on the receipt, Ex. CW1/X. It is firstly noted, that the style of signature of the Accused has not been deposed or brought on record by the Accused. Further, in any case, the handwriting/style of the signature on Ex. CW1/X closely resembles the one on the cheque, Ex. CW1/B; which is the admitted signature of the Accused. Be that as it may. It is noted that the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the Rohitbhai Case (supra) has observed that: "The observations of the Trial Court that there was no documentary evidence to show the source of funds with the Respondent to advance the loan, or that the Respondent did not record the transaction in the form of receipt of even kachcha notes, or that there were inconsistencies in the statement of the complainant and his witness, or that the witness of the complaint was more in know of facts etc. would have been relevant if the matter was to be examined with reference to the onus on the complaint to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt. These considerations and observations do not stand in conformity with the presumption existing in favour of the complainant by virtue of Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act. Needless to reiterate that the result of such presumption is that existence of a legally enforceable debt is to be presumed in favour of the complainant. When such a presumption is drawn, the factors relating to the want of documentary evidence in the Page 15 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 form of receipts or accounts or want of evidence as regards source of funds were not of relevant consideration while examining if the Accused has been able to rebut the presumption or not." Hence, even the arguments of the Accused as to the absence of any written receipt or receipt Ex.CW1/X being forged, do not help the Accused, as the Complainant is not required to produce documentary evidence in the first place, or to prove his case beyond all reasonable doubt. Hence, even if reliance is not placed on Ex. CW1/X; the case of the Complainant is not affected. It is further noted that the Complainant has in his cross examination stated that the children of the Accused were present at home at the time of handing over the cheque in question by the Accused to the Complainant. However, the Accused has not examined his children as well to evince the absence of the loan transaction/handing over the cheque in question to the Complainant. Accordingly, this defence of the Accused as to the absence of the loan transaction, also does not inspire confidence from the stand point of a reasonable man weighed against the standard of preponderance of probabilities. 27.In these circumstances and in view of the above detailed discussion, this court is of the considered opinion that the Accused has failed to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 in favour of the Complainant and ingredients of Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 are fully proved. Therefore, Accused is held guilty and convicted for commission of offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881. Let he be heard on the quantum of sentence on 20.12.2021 at 12:00 noon. Page 16 of 17 Banarshi Das Saini v. Inder, CC No.7310/2017 ORDER: CONVICTED Announced in Open Court (Twinkle Chawla) 07.12.2021 MM (NI-Act 02), South East Saket Court, New Delhi Note: This judgment contains 17 pages and each page has been signed by me. (Twinkle Chawla) MM (NI-Act 02), South East Saket Court, New Delhi Page 17 of 17
